Where is Denver and how big is the housing market?

Denver is the capital of Colorado and its largest city, sitting in the South Platte River valley just east of the Front Range. The Census Bureau counted 715,522 residents in 2020 and estimated 740,613 for July 1, 2025.

The city is also a county. Denver became a consolidated city and county in 1902, so one government handles both municipal services and the county duties of assessing, taxing and recording property. For a seller, that means fewer offices to deal with than in most Colorado towns.

All of these come from the Census Bureau's QuickFacts table for 2020 to 2024. Fewer than half of Denver homes are owner-occupied, so a good share of sellers here are landlords, heirs or people who bought a rental and want out.

How did Denver grow into the city it is today?

Denver was platted in 1858 where Cherry Creek meets the South Platte River, during the Pikes Peak gold rush. It was named for Kansas Territorial Governor James W. Denver, incorporated as Denver City in 1861 and shortened to Denver in 1866.

It became the territorial capital in 1867, and an 1881 referendum made it the permanent state capital.

Elevation is officially 5,280 feet, the source of the Mile High nickname. The city covers roughly 153 square miles of land and is divided into 78 official neighborhoods used for planning, including LoDo, RiNo, Park Hill, Uptown, the Golden Triangle and Central Park, which was formerly Stapleton.

Who employs people in Denver?

Government, health care, education and aviation lead the list of Denver's largest employers. The city's own 2023 financial report names these five at the top:

  • City and County of Denver: 13,584 employees
  • Denver Public Schools: 12,693
  • State of Colorado: 10,686
  • Denver Health and Hospital Authority: 9,502
  • United Airlines: 7,230

The Denver metro area's gross metropolitan product was $311.9 billion in 2023, and eight Fortune 500 companies have headquarters in the city. Census data shows 74.2% of Denver residents aged 16 and over are in the civilian labor force, and the mean commute is 24.9 minutes.

Steady public-sector and hospital jobs keep demand for housing close to downtown, but they do not protect an individual owner from a job loss, a divorce or an inherited house that nobody wants to manage.

What does Denver weather mean for a house?

Hail is the weather risk that matters most for Denver roofs. Denver ranks 10th among U.S. cities with at least 50,000 people for hail proneness and has had three of the ten costliest hailstorms in the country.

The climate is cool and semi-arid, with about 3,100 hours of sunshine a year and average snowfall of 53.5 inches. July highs average 89.9 degrees, and the record high is 105 degrees, set June 28, 2018.

A hail-damaged roof, cracked siding or an unrepaired insurance claim can slow a traditional sale, because buyers' lenders and inspectors look hard at roofs. Sellers in Denver often face these questions:

  • Was the hail damage ever claimed and repaired, or just left?
  • How old is the roof, and will a buyer's insurer cover it?
  • Do sun and freeze-thaw cycles show up in the stucco, deck or exterior paint?

How do property taxes work when you sell a Denver house?

Denver taxes are billed after the year they cover, and the city's Treasury Division collects them. The Treasury page lists two ways to pay: two installments, due the last day of February and June 15, or a single payment due April 30. If a due date lands on a weekend or holiday, it moves to the next business day.

Statements are now online. An owner searches the address in Denver's property search tool, opens the Tax Documents section and downloads the statement for the year. Paying by credit or debit card carries a 2.5% service fee, while an electronic check avoids it. Treasury's phone number is 720-913-9300.

At a closing, the title company usually prorates the current year's taxes between seller and buyer. Treasury also offers a Certificate of Taxes Due for Real Property, a document title companies use to confirm what is owed on a parcel. Unpaid prior years must be cleared before a clean transfer.

For appeal rights and assessment timing, see the Denver Treasury property tax page.

What is the state fee when a Denver deed is recorded?

Colorado charges a documentary fee of $0.01 per $100 on transfer deeds where the consideration is more than $500. County recording pages describe it that way, and on a $500,000 sale it works out to $50.

Denver records deeds in the same county system, so the fee, the recording charge and any transfer paperwork appear on the settlement statement. A cash sale does not change these steps, but it can shorten the time between signing and recording because no lender has to fund the loan first.

What rental and short-term rental rules affect Denver sellers?

Denver requires a license for every short-term rental, and the rental must be the host's primary residence. Hosts also have to show their business license number in every advertisement, and those who break the rules can be fined or lose the license.

That rule matters if you own a second Denver property that was operating as an Airbnb. A primary-residence requirement means a non-owner-occupied house cannot lawfully run as a short-term rental, so the house may have to be sold or converted to a long-term rental. The same house can be worth less to a buyer who counted on nightly rental income.

The city's rental, zoning and licensing pages are the place to confirm what applies to your address before you list or accept an offer.

What are the ways to sell a Denver house?

Most Denver owners choose among three routes: list with an agent, sell on their own, or accept a cash purchase. Each route trades price against time and effort.

  • Listing with an agent: usually the highest sale price on a house in good condition, but with showings, repairs requested after inspection and a buyer's loan approval to wait for.
  • Selling on your own: saves the agent's commission but leaves pricing, disclosures and paperwork to you.
  • Cash sale: a buyer purchases the house as it stands, so there is no repair list and a closing date you can often choose.

A cash route fits a house with deferred maintenance, a hail-damaged roof, a tenant in place or an estate that needs to settle. A listing usually fits a clean house with time on the calendar. You can compare both before deciding, and a cash offer from us carries no obligation.

How much is the median home worth in Denver?

The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figure for the median value of owner-occupied homes in Denver is $616,000. Individual houses vary a great deal with condition, neighborhood and lot size, so treat it as a citywide benchmark and not a price for your house.

When are Denver property taxes due?

Denver's Treasury page lists the last day of February and June 15 for two installments, or April 30 for one full payment. A due date on a weekend or holiday moves to the next business day.

Can I sell a Denver house that was used as a short-term rental?

Yes. Denver's rules require a license and a primary-residence host, so a house that lacked either may have compliance issues a buyer will ask about. A cash buyer can purchase it as it stands, though you should settle any city fines or unpaid taxes.

Does hail damage stop me from selling a house in Denver?

No. Denver is among the most hail-prone large cities, so buyers expect to see it. A damaged roof can lower the price or complicate a buyer's financing, which is why many owners with roof damage consider an as-is cash sale.

What is the state documentary fee in Colorado?

It is $0.01 per $100 of consideration on a deed over $500, as county recording pages describe it. On a $500,000 sale that is $50.

Where is Colorado Springs and how large is it?

Colorado Springs is the county seat of El Paso County, about 70 miles south of Denver on Fountain Creek, near the base of Pikes Peak. It covers 195.761 square miles, the largest area of any Colorado municipality.

The Census Bureau counted 478,961 residents in 2020, up from 416,427 in 2010, and estimated 494,743 for July 1, 2025. That makes it the second most populous city in the state. The city sits at about 6,011 feet, which is roughly 700 feet higher than Denver.

What is the history of Colorado Springs in brief?

The area began with Colorado City, organized August 13, 1859, during the Pikes Peak gold rush. Fountain Colony was renamed Colorado Springs in 1871, the county seat moved over in 1873, and the town was incorporated on June 19, 1886.

The military arrived later and shaped the modern city. Camp Carson, now Fort Carson, was established in 1941. In 1950 Ent Air Force Base was chosen as the Air Defense Command headquarters, and Peterson Field reopened as an Air Force base in 1951. Most of the former Ent base became a U.S. Olympic training center in 1977.

The city's government changed in 2010, when it adopted a council and strong mayor system. The nine-member council has six district seats and three at-large members.

Which employers drive the Colorado Springs economy?

The military, high-tech industry and tourism lead the local economy, in that order. Wikipedia reports about 45,000 active-duty troops in the area as of 2021, plus more than 100,000 veterans, and says the military and defense contractors supply more than 40% of the Pikes Peak region's economy.

  • Installations: Fort Carson, the U.S. Air Force Academy, Peterson Space Force Base, Schriever Space Force Base and Cheyenne Mountain Space Force Station.
  • Defense contractors named include Northrop Grumman, Boeing, General Dynamics, L3Harris and Lockheed Martin.
  • Tourism supplies more than 16,000 jobs in the region.

Unemployment was 4.6% in April 2025. Military and defense employment is a large part of the local economy, so buyer demand can shift with major employer decisions.

What does the Colorado Springs climate and wildfire history mean for a house?

Colorado Springs has a semi-arid climate with about 243 sunny days a year, around 16.5 inches of precipitation and 38 inches of snow in an average season. March is the snowiest month, and most of the rain arrives in July and August with the monsoon.

The city averages 18 days a year at or above 90 degrees and 5.2 nights below zero. It is also among the most active lightning-strike areas in the country. Those swings in temperature stress roofs, gutters, decks and exterior paint.

Wildfire is part of the city's recent memory. The Waldo Canyon fire began June 23, 2012, about 4 miles northwest of the city, destroyed 347 homes within the city and forced 32,000 residents to evacuate. The Black Forest fire the next year was more destructive. Owners should ask their insurer how wildfire risk is treated for their address.

El Paso County bills and collects taxes on Colorado Springs property. The county Treasurer's Important Dates page lists these steps in the cycle:

  • January 28: statements must be mailed.
  • Last day of February: the first half is due.
  • April 30: the full-year payment option is due.
  • June 15: the second half is due, and unpaid taxes become delinquent afterward.

Delinquent real estate taxes are advertised in September and sold at public auction in October. After September 30 the Treasurer requires cash or certified funds. A deadline on a weekend or legal holiday carries to the next business day.

At closing the title company calculates what the seller owes through the closing date. Any tax lien from a prior year must be redeemed first, and redemption payments must reach the Treasurer by the last business day of the month. Read the El Paso County Treasurer's dates page for the current year.

What are the short-term rental rules in Colorado Springs?

Colorado Springs requires a permit for any rental of 29 days or less. The permit costs $124.95, lasts one year and must be renewed without a lapse, because the city says there is no grace period.

Applicants must show proof of primary residence, at least $500,000 in liability insurance and a link to their hosting platform listing. Two separate units on one property need two separate permits. City staff has 10 business days to review a complete application. For a non-owner-occupied rental, a lapsed permit can mean forfeiture of the established permit, which affects what a buyer will pay for a house sold as a rental business.

Interstate 25 runs through the city for nearly 18 miles, and Powers Boulevard (State Highway 21) is a major semi-expressway on the east side. Other routes include Highways 83, 94 and 115, U.S. 24 and U.S. 85.

Colorado Springs Airport, open since 1925, is the second-largest commercial airport in Colorado and handled 2,134,618 passengers in 2022. Named areas include Old Colorado City, Broadmoor, Ivywild, Knob Hill, Roswell, the Old North End and Banning Lewis Ranch. Mean travel time to work was 22.7 minutes in 2020 to 2024 Census data, and sellers can point to that when describing a house near the interstate or Powers.

You can list with an agent, sell it yourself or accept a cash purchase, and the right choice depends on condition and timing. Military families with orders, heirs settling an estate and landlords with a vacant rental often put speed first.

  • A cash purchase is as-is, so repairs, wear and a hail or fire-season insurance question do not hold up closing.

The first half is due the last day of February, the full-year option on or before April 30 and the second half June 15. The Treasurer's page says unpaid taxes become delinquent after the second half deadline.

Do I need a permit to rent my Colorado Springs house on Airbnb?

Yes, for stays of 29 days or less. The city's permit is $124.95, lasts one year and requires proof of primary residence and $500,000 in liability insurance.

How big is Aurora and where does it sit?

Aurora is a home rule city in Arapahoe, Adams and Douglas counties, and it is a principal city of the Denver metro area. It covers about 163.6 square miles, which makes it second in Colorado by land area and roughly 6% larger than Denver.

How did Aurora get its name?

The area was platted around 1890 or 1891 as Fletcher, after Denver businessman Donald Fletcher, and incorporated as the Town of Fletcher on May 5, 1903. It was renamed Aurora in 1907 after one of its subdivisions.

It reincorporated as a city on March 9, 1928, and became one of the fastest growing cities in the country in the late 1970s and early 1980s. That growth explains why so much of its housing is from the 1970s and later.

Most of Aurora sits in Arapahoe County, which was founded November 1, 1861, covers 805 square miles and had 655,070 residents in 2020, making it the third most populous county in Colorado. Littleton is the county seat, and Aurora is the largest city.

The county stretches 72 miles east to west but only 4 to 12 miles north to south, and it is 97.9% urban. Other cities in it include Centennial, Englewood, Greenwood Village and Cherry Hills Village, so a buyer comparing homes may be weighing several neighboring tax districts at once.

Adams and Douglas county addresses follow their own offices, and your bill and closing paperwork come from the one that matches your parcel.

How did Erie start, and does the coal history still affect houses?

Erie began as a coal town. Coal turned up in the mid-1860s in the southwest corner of Weld County, and the town took its name from Erie, Pennsylvania, the old home of early settler Richard Van Valkenburg.

Railroads arrived in 1870 and 1871 and carried coal toward Denver and nearby communities. The first official underground mine opened in 1876 under Ira Austin. Unlike a temporary mining camp, miners here owned homes in town.

Wikipedia notes that the school has paused open enrollment because of overcapacity, so students outside its attendance zone are not admitted.   • Farmers' markets are allowed in any zone district except residential areas where the main use is a single or two-family home, and they need a business license.

Because the city touches Broomfield and Erie, a house with a Lafayette mailing address can sit in a different jurisdiction than you expect. Check the address against city limits before you assume which rules apply.

How did Lafayette begin, and why does coal still matter?

Lafayette was founded in 1888 by Mary E. Miller, who platted the town on part of the farm she and her husband Lafayette Miller had bought in 1868. Coal was discovered on the Miller farm in 1884, and the first Simpson Mine shaft was sunk in 1887.

The town became part of the Northern Coal Field boom that supplied Denver's households, smelters and power plants. Lafayette's last mine, the Black Diamond at today's US 287 and Baseline Road, closed in 1956, and the city shifted back to farming before suburban growth took over. Very little of the mining past remains, though a few structures moved from the mine camps still stand in Old Town.
